  "claims": [
    {
      "id":"f1","concept_id":"c1",
      "text":"A checkpoint transfers transactions from the WAL file back into the database.",
      "source_id":"S1",
      "quote":"Moving the WAL file transactions back into the database is called a \" checkpoint \".",
      "pass":0
    },
    {
      "id":"f2","concept_id":"c2",
      "text":"sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint(D,N) triggers automatic checkpointing after a transaction commits if the WAL contains at least N frames.",
      "source_id":"S3",
      "quote":"automatically checkpoint after committing a transaction if there are N or more frames in the write-ahead log file.",
      "pass":0
    },
    {
      "id":"f3","concept_id":"c2",
      "text":"Passing N equal to zero or a negative value to sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint disables automatic checkpoints.",
      "source_id":"S3",
      "quote":"Passing zero or a negative value as the N parameter disables automatic checkpoints entirely.",
      "pass":0
    },
    {
      "id":"f4","concept_id":"c2",
      "text":"Every new database connection enables automatic checkpointing with a default threshold of 1000 pages or the SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT setting.",
      "source_id":"S3",
      "quote":"Every new database connection defaults to having the auto-checkpoint enabled with a threshold of 1000 or SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT pages.",
      "pass":0
    },
    {
      "id":"f5","concept_id":"c2",
      "text":"Checkpoints initiated through sqlite3_wal_checkpoint() or the automatic checkpoint mechanism use PASSIVE mode.",
      "source_id":"S1",
      "quote":"All checkpoints initiated by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint() and by the automatic checkpoint mechanism are PASSIVE.",
      "pass":0
    },
    {
      "id":"f6","concept_id":"c3",
      "text":"Configuring sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint replaces any existing sqlite3_wal_hook callback.",
      "source_id":"S3",
      "quote":"The callback registered by this function replaces any existing callback registered using sqlite3_wal_hook() .",
      "pass":0
    },
    {
      "id":"f7","concept_id":"c3",
      "text":"Registering a sqlite3_wal_hook callback disables automatic checkpointing configured by sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint.",
      "source_id":"S3",
      "quote":"Likewise, registering a callback using sqlite3_wal_hook() disables the automatic checkpoint mechanism configured by this function.",
      "pass":0
    },
    {
      "id":"f8","concept_id":"c4",
      "text":"A checkpoint can run concurrently with readers but must stop at a WAL page beyond any current reader's end mark.",
      "source_id":"S1",
      "quote":"A checkpoint can run concurrently with readers, however the checkpoint must stop when it reaches a page in the WAL that is past the end mark of any current reader.",
      "pass":0
    },
    {
      "id":"f9","concept_id":"c4",
      "text":"A checkpoint records its progress in the wal-index and resumes from that position on its next invocation.",
      "source_id":"S1",
      "quote":"The checkpoint remembers (in the wal-index) how far it got and will resume transferring content from the WAL to the database from where it left off on the next invocation.",
      "pass":0
    },
    {
      "id":"f10","concept_id":"c4",
      "text":"Continuously overlapping readers can prevent checkpoint completion and allow the WAL file to grow without bound.",
      "source_id":"S1",
      "quote":"if a database has many concurrent overlapping readers and there is always at least one active reader, then no checkpoints will be able to complete and hence the WAL file will grow without bound.",
      "pass":0
    },
    {
      "id":"f11","concept_id":"c4",
      "text":"Attempting checkpoints during reader-free gaps can avoid checkpoint starvation.",
      "source_id":"S1",
      "quote":"This scenario can be avoided by ensuring that there are \"reader gaps\": times when no processes are reading from the database and that checkpoints are attempted during those times.",
      "pass":0
    },
    {
      "id":"f12","concept_id":"c5",
      "text":"A checkpoint normally recycles the WAL without truncating its physical file; journal_size_limit can change that behavior.",
      "source_id":"S1",
      "quote":"The checkpoint does not normally truncate the WAL file (unless the journal_size_limit pragma is set). Instead, it merely causes SQLite to start overwriting the WAL file from the beginning.",
      "pass":0
    },
    {
      "id":"f13","concept_id":"c5",
      "text":"The WAL file cannot be reset in the middle of a write transaction.",
      "source_id":"S1",
      "quote":"A checkpoint can only complete when no other transactions are running, which means the WAL file cannot be reset in the middle of a write transaction.",
      "pass":0
    },
    {
      "id":"f14","concept_id":"c6",
      "text":"The WAL must be synced to persistent storage before checkpointing moves its content into the database.",
      "source_id":"S1",
      "quote":"The WAL must be synced to persistent storage prior to moving content from the WAL into the database",
      "pass":0
    },
    {
      "id":"f15","concept_id":"c6",
      "text":"The database file must be synced before the WAL is reset.",
      "source_id":"S1",
      "quote":"and the database file must be synced prior to resetting the WAL.",
      "pass":0
    },
    {
      "id":"f16","concept_id":"c7",
      "text":"By default, the thread performing the COMMIT that pushes the WAL over its size limit also runs the automatic checkpoint.",
      "source_id":"S1",
      "quote":"By default, the checkpoint will be run automatically by the same thread that does the COMMIT that pushes the WAL over its size limit.",
      "pass":0
    },
    {
      "id":"f17","concept_id":"c7",
      "text":"Under the default scheduling strategy, commits that trigger checkpoints can be much slower than other commits.",
      "source_id":"S1",
      "quote":"This has the effect of causing most COMMIT operations to be very fast but an occasional COMMIT (those that trigger a checkpoint) to be much slower.",
      "pass":0
    },
    {
      "id":"f18","concept_id":"c8",
      "text":"SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE checkpoints as many frames as possible without waiting for readers or writers and syncs the database file if it checkpoints all log frames.",

      "quote":"SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE Checkpoint as many frames as possible without waiting for any database readers or writers to finish, then sync the database file if all frames in the log were checkpointed.",

    },

      "id":"f19","concept_id":"c8",
      "text":"SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE never invokes the busy-handler callback.",
      "source_id":"S2",
      "quote":"The busy-handler callback is never invoked in the SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE mode. On the other hand, passive mode might leave the checkpoint unfinished if there are concurrent readers or writers.",

    },

      "id":"f20","concept_id":"c9",
      "text":"SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL waits through the busy handler for no active database writer and for all readers to use the most recent database snapshot, subject to busy-handler termination.",
      "source_id":"S2",
      "quote":"SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL This mode blocks (it invokes the busy-handler callback ) until there is no database writer and all readers are reading from the most recent database snapshot.",

    },

      "id":"f21","concept_id":"c9",
      "text":"After satisfying its waiting conditions, SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL checkpoints all log frames and syncs the database file.",

      "quote":"It then checkpoints all frames in the log file and syncs the database file.",

    },

      "id":"f22","concept_id":"c9",
      "text":"A pending SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL blocks new database writers while allowing new database readers to continue unimpeded.",

      "quote":"This mode blocks new database writers while it is pending, but new database readers are allowed to continue unimpeded.",

      "id":"f23","concept_id":"c10",
      "text":"SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART adds a post-checkpoint wait for all readers to read only from the database file, subject to busy-handler termination.",

    },

      "id":"f24","concept_id":"c10",
      "text":"Successfully satisfying the RESTART reader condition ensures that the next writer restarts the log from its beginning.",

      "quote":"This ensures that the next writer will restart the log file from the beginning.",
      "pass":0
    },

      "id":"f25","concept_id":"c10",
      "text":"A pending SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART blocks new writer attempts but does not impede readers according to the dedicated API reference.",

      "quote":"Like SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL, this mode blocks new database writer attempts while it is pending, but does not impede readers.",
      "pass":0
    },

      "id":"f26","concept_id":"c11",
      "text":"SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE follows RESTART behavior and additionally truncates the log to zero bytes just before a successful return.",

      "quote":"SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE This mode works the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART with the addition that it also truncates the log file to zero bytes just prior to a successful return.",
      "pass":0
    },
    {
      "id":"f27","concept_id":"c12",
      "text":"SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_NOOP checkpoints zero frames and serves to retrieve pnLog and pnCkpt status values.",

      "pass":0
    },
    {
      "id":"f28","concept_id":"c13",
      "text":"All sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2 calls require an exclusive checkpoint lock; a concurrent checkpoint preventing lock acquisition causes SQLITE_BUSY.",
      "source_id":"S2",
      "quote":"All calls obtain an exclusive \"checkpoint\" lock on the database file. If any other process is running a checkpoint operation at the same time, the lock cannot be obtained and SQLITE_BUSY is returned.",
      "pass":0
    },
    {
      "id":"f29","concept_id":"c13",
      "text":"Checkpoint-lock contention does not invoke the busy handler even when one is configured.",
      "source_id":"S2",
      "quote":"Even if there is a busy-handler configured, it will not be invoked in this case.",
      "pass":0
    },
    {
      "id":"f30","concept_id":"c13",
      "text":"SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL, SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART and SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE also acquire the exclusive writer lock.",
      "source_id":"S2",
      "quote":"The SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL, RESTART and TRUNCATE modes also obtain the exclusive \"writer\" lock on the database file.",
      "pass":0
    },
    {
      "id":"f31","concept_id":"c13",
      "text":"If the busy handler returns zero before writer-lock acquisition or while waiting for readers, checkpointing falls back to PASSIVE behavior.",
      "source_id":"S2",
      "quote":"If the busy-handler returns 0 before the writer lock is obtained or while waiting for database readers, the checkpoint operation proceeds from that point in the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE",
      "pass":0
    },
    {
      "id":"f32","concept_id":"c13",
      "text":"The busy-handler termination fallback returns SQLITE_BUSY rather than guaranteeing successful checkpoint completion.",
      "source_id":"S2",
      "quote":"checkpointing as many frames as possible without blocking any further. SQLITE_BUSY is returned in this case.",
      "pass":0
    },
    {
      "id":"f33","concept_id":"c14",
      "text":"For a selected database, a non-null pnLog receives the total log frame count, or -1 when an error or non-WAL mode prevents the checkpoint from running.",
      "source_id":"S2",
      "quote":"If pnLog is not NULL, then *pnLog is set to the total number of frames in the log file or to -1 if the checkpoint could not run because of an error or because the database is not in WAL",
      "pass":0
    },
    {
      "id":"f34","concept_id":"c14",
      "text":"For a selected database, pnCkpt counts all checkpointed frames in the log, including frames checkpointed before the current call.",
      "source_id":"S2",
      "quote":"*pnCkpt is set to the total number of checkpointed frames in the log file (including any that were already checkpointed before the function was called)",
      "pass":0
    },
    {
      "id":"f35","concept_id":"c15",
      "text":"A null or empty zDb requests the operation on all WAL databases attached to the connection.",
      "source_id":"S2",
      "quote":"If parameter zDb is NULL or points to a zero length string, then the specified operation is attempted on all WAL databases attached to database connection db.",
      "pass":0
    },
    {
      "id":"f36","concept_id":"c15",
      "text":"When zDb selects all attached WAL databases, pnLog and pnCkpt output values are undefined.",
      "source_id":"S2",
      "quote":"In this case the values written to output parameters *pnLog and *pnCkpt are undefined.",
      "pass":0
    }

limitations: The three supplied sources are SQLite documentation from one origin; they do not satisfy an independent-origin authority floor.

The dedicated API reference S2 governs exact mode semantics over S1's overview: S2 documents PASSIVE, FULL, RESTART, TRUNCATE and NOOP, while S1's application-initiated overview lists only three modes and later mentions RESET.
S1 says RESTART and TRUNCATE ensure completion before returning; S2 qualifies this with busy-handler termination, PASSIVE fallback and SQLITE_BUSY, so unconditional completion is not accepted.
S1 warns that RESTART and TRUNCATE might block readers, while S2 explicitly says RESTART does not impede readers and defines TRUNCATE through RESTART; the packet does not explain this discrepancy.
No independent evidence establishes the history or cause of the documentation discrepancies, and no unsupported reconciliation is asserted.
Only one bounded extraction pass was performed; the information rate is new accepted claims divided by accepted claims in that pass, not evidence of research saturation.
The 36-claim output cap limits coverage; no external retrieval, live inventory inspection, installation or verification was performed.
